gloss.v: The share of a group of people who die over a period of time, whatever the cause. The book uses it to measure how long people live. Abbreviated ACM in studies.

Hazard ratio. Over the same period, how fast the group that did something had the outcome (death, illness), divided by the group that didn't. HR 0.87 means 13% lower than the group that didn't; HR 1.21 means 21% higher.
Relative risk. The ratio of the chance of the outcome in two groups; read it the same way as HR.
Odds ratio. Also compares two groups, calculated slightly differently from RR: when the outcome is rare it is close to RR; when the outcome is common it overstates the gap.
Incidence rate ratio. Incidence is the share of people newly getting a disease over a period; divide the two groups and read it like RR.
Rate ratio. Compares how many times something happened (for example, how many falls), not how many people it happened to; read it like RR.
SMR. How many people in this group actually died, divided by how many people of the same age would normally be expected to die. 5.86 means 5.86 times as many deaths as their peers.
Subtract the two groups' risks to get "how many extra per thousand people". A ratio only says how many times higher; the risk difference says how many more people, in real numbers.

95% confidence interval. Any number a study calculates has error; this is the range the true value most likely falls in. If the range of a ratio crosses 1, or the range of a difference crosses 0, the gap between the groups may be chance, and the text says "not statistically significant".

Randomised controlled trial. People are split into two groups by something like drawing lots; one group does the thing and the other doesn't, then the outcomes are compared. It is the most convincing way to show that the thing itself made the difference.
Pools the results of many studies and recalculates them into one overall number.
Cohort study. A large group of people is followed for many years and outcomes are recorded. It can show that two things often go together, but cannot prove that the first caused the second.

Observational study. Researchers only record; they don't assign who does what. Results are easily skewed by other factors (see confounding and reverse causation in this table), so take the numbers with a pinch of salt.

A third factor drives both the cause and the effect, making two things look causally linked. For example, people who eat more vegetables also tend to exercise more, so it is hard to tell which one is doing the work.
Cause and effect run the other way: it looks as if the first causes the second, but the second causes the first. Sleeping a lot doesn't kill people early; seriously ill people sleep a lot.
Effect size: how big the gap between two groups is, expressed as multiples of the usual spread. 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
Correlation coefficient. How closely two things move together, from -1 to 1; 0.1 is weak, 0.3 moderate, 0.5 strong.
A unit of exercise intensity. Sitting quietly is 1 MET; brisk walking is about 3 to 4 MET. MET·h is intensity times hours, the total amount of activity.
A widely used international system that rates how reliable a body of evidence is: high, moderate, low or very low.
Effects are counted by who was invited to screening, not by who actually went. Some invited people never go, so this method understates the benefit for those who do get screened.
A unit for how much someone has smoked in total: packs per day times years smoked. 30 pack-years means a pack a day for 30 years.
Body mass index, a common measure of weight: weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, the so-called bad cholesterol.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate, a measure of how well the kidneys filter, in mL/min/1.73 m². Lower means worse kidney function; the stages of chronic kidney disease are defined by it.
Hepatitis B surface antigen, an item on lab reports. A positive result means infection with the hepatitis B virus.
Human papillomavirus. There are many types; long-term infection with some of them can cause cervical cancer.
Low-dose chest CT, with about one-fifth to one-tenth of the radiation of a standard CT.
Fine particles floating in the air, 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter.
A food classification system that sorts foods into four groups by how heavily processed they are; "ultra-processed food" is the fourth group.
Loan Prime Rate. China's benchmark lending rate, published on the 20th of each month; mortgage rates and the legal cap on private-loan interest are based on it.
In certain labour arbitration cases the award takes effect immediately and the employer cannot take the matter to court again.

The number of couples registering a marriage or a divorce per thousand people in a year. The divorce-to-marriage ratio (divorces divided by marriages in the same year) is a different number; don't mix them up.
Automated external defibrillator. The red or yellow first-aid box found in public places; switch it on and follow the voice prompts, and it decides by itself whether to shock.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Pressing hard on the chest during cardiac arrest to keep blood flowing.
China Compulsory Certification. Products on the list may not leave the factory or be sold without this mark.
A registration with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology's system before a website or app officially goes live in China.
China's cybersecurity classified protection system. Systems are graded by importance; the higher the grade, the more security measures are required.
An open-source licence. If you build something with code under it and distribute it, you usually have to publish your own code too.
An agreement with your employer not to work for a competitor for a period after leaving. The company must pay you monthly compensation during that period, for at most 2 years.
The money you promise to invest when registering a company. Once promised, it must actually be paid in within the legal deadline; it is not just a number for show.

Two Chinese terms one character apart (dìngjīn and dìngjīn) with very different legal effect: an earnest deposit carries a penalty, so the party that received it must refund double if they back out, capped at 20% of the contract value; an advance payment is just money paid early, with no such penalty.

rd.术语表导语: The text uses everyday language where possible, but citing studies inevitably brings in a few statistical terms. Look them up here; on the search page, hover over a word with a dotted underline (tap on mobile) to see its explanation.

3-17.human: Reframing what just happened, or putting yourself in the other person's shoes, both calm emotions down, and the second works better. Simply not showing the emotion helps a little; forcibly suppressing the feeling or forcing yourself not to think about it doesn't work. People who punished the offender kept ruminating on it for longer afterwards; those who didn't retaliate moved on faster.
3-17.gain: A meta-analysis of 306 experimental comparisons: reinterpreting what happened (cognitive reappraisal) had an effect size of d = 0.36 on emotion; taking the other person's perspective d = 0.45; distraction d = 0.27. Suppressing the outward expression of emotion worked, d = 0.32. Suppressing the feeling itself did not (d = -0.04), nor did trying not to think about the event (d = -0.12). These figures combine subjective feelings, outward expression and physiological measures; the abstract does not report them separately. Three further experiments showed that people who punished an offender ruminated about them longer afterwards, while those who didn't punish moved on faster. People overestimate in advance how satisfying revenge will be.

6-19.note: What is ruled out is starting lifelong urate-lowering drugs without ever having had an attack; it doesn't mean high uric acid is harmless. The same guideline lists exceptions where starting can be considered: a first attack together with stage 3 or higher chronic kidney disease; serum urate above 9 mg/dL (about 535 µmol/L); or a history of kidney stones. People who have already had attacks, have tophi, or show bone erosion on imaging should take the drug; see section 16, item 9. About 7.4% of Han Chinese carry the HLA-B*5801 genotype, versus 0.7% of white people. Carriers who take allopurinol are more likely to develop a severe, potentially fatal drug rash; Asian patients face three times the risk of hypersensitivity syndrome compared with white patients. Since this is a drug you can hold off on anyway, there is no reason to take that extra risk; get tested for the genotype before starting, see section 16, item 9. The two kidney trials enrolled people with chronic kidney disease and type 1 diabetes, so they cannot be generalised to "high uric acid is completely harmless to the kidneys"; they only rule out the idea that lowering uric acid with drugs protects the kidneys.

16-9.note: Controversy: guidelines differ on which urate-lowering drug to use. US guidelines prefer allopurinol and advise people with cardiovascular disease to avoid febuxostat where possible, but the European FAST trial did not find febuxostat more dangerous. Benzbromarone, a drug that increases uric acid excretion, is also available in China. The Chinese Medical Association guidelines (2019 and the 2024 update) give separate recommendations on drug choice and urine alkalinisation. Whether to add sodium bicarbonate with benzbromarone has no supporting evidence according to US guidelines; follow your doctor's advice, and drinking plenty of water is a must. People of Han Chinese ancestry should consider testing for HLA-B*5801 before taking allopurinol. It is an inherited immune-response genotype; one test is valid for life. Carriers make up 7.4% of Han Chinese, Korean and Thai people, versus 0.7% of white and Hispanic people. After taking allopurinol, Asian and African patients face three times the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome compared with white patients; in severe cases large areas of skin peel off and it can be fatal. The American College of Rheumatology's 2020 gout guideline suggests these groups consider testing first. Starting urate-lowering therapy can actually trigger attacks, so guidelines require taking an anti-inflammatory preventive drug for the first 3 to 6 months. "The urate-lowering drug made it hurt more, so I stopped" is the most common way this fails; when it flares, add anti-inflammatories as prescribed instead of stopping the urate-lowering drug. Targets are written differently: below 6 mg/dL is about 360 µmol/L, and Chinese lab reports mostly use µmol/L. High uric acid found at a check-up without any attack is a different matter; see section 6, item 19. For sugary drinks and alcohol see section 2, items 7 and 19.

23-6.t: Treat "study or start working" as a calculation: three years of earlier wages from working now, against decades of higher annual income from studying longer
23-6.human: Starting work earlier earns a few extra years of wages, but only once. Studying longer earns a bit more every year for thirty or forty years. So compare the two sums side by side. In urban China, each extra year of schooling raises annual income by roughly 4.0% to 10.2%, but these figures are from before 2001 and only give a rough idea.
